title: Tagliatelle al Tartufo
subtitle: egg tagliatelle with black truffle and butter
excerpt: Tagliatelle al tartufo dresses egg pasta with truffle-infused butter, Parmesan, and freshly shaved or grated black truffle. The technique is the same as fettuccine Alfredo: quality butter emulsified with pasta water, with truffle as the dominant flavour. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Tagliatelle with truffle is the defining pasta of the truffle-growing regions of central Italy: Norcia and Spoleto in Umbria (black truffle, Tuber melanosporum), and Alba and the Langhe in Piedmont (white truffle, Tuber magnatum). The preparation is identical for both: hot egg pasta dressed with the best butter and finely shaved or grated truffle. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), documents pasta dressed with truffle and butter as a standard of Italian festive cooking. The white truffle version (Piedmont, autumn) is more expensive and more aromatic; the black truffle version (Umbria, winter and late autumn) is more accessible and cooks more robustly. Both share the same rule: the truffle goes on at the last moment and receives no direct heat.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Truffle loses its aroma quickly. Buy it as close to serving as possible and do not prepare the dish ahead.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Périgord or Norcia black truffle, harvested from December to March. It has an earthy, musky, slightly chocolatey aroma. Fresh black truffle can be grated directly over pasta. Truffle oil is not a substitute: most commercial truffle oil contains synthetic 2,4-dithiapentane and lacks truffle flavour.

content.text: Tagliatelle al tartufo is not a complex dish. It is butter and Parmesan pasta, the same technique as Alfredo, with truffle added at the last moment. Cold butter emulsified with pasta water and the pasta's starch creates a glossy coating. The truffle goes in off the heat, shaved or grated over the top so the warmth draws out its aroma without cooking it.

A fresh truffle is necessary here. Truffle oil made with synthetic compounds tastes artificial and obvious. If fresh truffle is not available, preserved whole truffle in brine or oil (Tuber melanosporum) is a distant but workable substitute.

items.prepNote: fresh, cleaned; or 30 g preserved in brine
white pepper optional, to not mark the truffle

content.text: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Cook {{pasta-fresh}} of fresh tagliatelle for 2 to 3 minutes until just al dente. Reserve 200 ml of pasta cooking water.

Place a large saute pan over medium heat. Add 100 ml of pasta cooking water and {{unsalted-butter}} of cold cubed butter. Swirl until the butter melts and emulsifies into the water, about 1 minute. The sauce should look creamy, not separated.

Drain the pasta and add to the pan. Toss vigorously for 1 minute. Remove from heat. Add {{parmesan}} of Parmesan in two additions, tossing between each, with a splash of pasta water if the sauce tightens.
Divide between warm bowls. Shave or grate {{
-truffle-fresh}} of truffle directly over each bowl. Serve immediately; the truffle aroma dissipates within minutes of contact with heat.

items.symptom: Truffle aroma is faint or disappears quickly
items.cause: Truffle not fresh enough, or applied to pasta that had cooled
items.fix: Truffle must be used the day it is bought. Apply to piping hot pasta at the table. The heat volatilises the aromatic compounds.

items.cause: Pan too hot or butter added all at once
items.fix: The pan must be medium, not high. Add butter to pasta water, not to a dry pan. Swirl rather than stir.

content.text: Tagliatelle al tartufo is eaten wherever Italian truffles are grown. In Norcia (Umbria), December and January bring the black truffle season. Local restaurants serve pasta, game, and truffle. In Alba (Piedmont), the white truffle season in October and November is a civic event: the Fiera del Tartufo draws buyers and chefs from across Europe. Tagliatelle al tartufo bianco from Alba is one of the finest things Italian cooking produces. In both cases the rule is the same: the simpler the dish, the more the truffle speaks.
